title: 2024 Smart‑Meter Electricity Consumption Report
executive_summary: The 2024 smart‑meter dataset captures 1,428 readings totaling 1.21 GWh of electricity use. Industrial sites account for the overwhelming majority of consumption, while peak‑time usage is roughly equal to off‑peak. Consumption rose modestly in the second half of the year, and on hot days commercial demand remains relatively low. These insights help prioritize demand‑side management and tariff strategies.

key_findings.statement: The dataset contains 1,428 readings with a total electricity consumption of 1,207,699.96 kWh, averaging about 845.73 kWh per reading.
Industrial buildings dominate electricity use, consuming roughly 995,362.16 kWh, followed by Commercial at 196,367.15 kWh, and Residential at 15,970.65 kWh.
Quarterly consumption peaked in Q4 with 352,881.81 kWh, then Q1 (319,677.67 kWh), Q2 (270,277.36 kWh), and Q3 (264,863.12 kWh).
Second‑half consumption (H2) was 617,744.93 kWh, a 4.71 % increase over the first half (H1 = 589,955.03 kWh), representing an absolute rise of 27,789.90 kWh.
On hot days (≥ 25 °C) there were 19 Commercial readings, averaging 415.29 kWh each.

Across all readings, the median consumption is 406.8 kWh with a standard deviation of 913.44 kWh. The average temperature recorded is 11.61 °C, with 62 readings missing temperature data. For Commercial meters, consumption and temperature are negatively correlated (‑0.64).

Peak‑time usage accounts for 49.65 % of total consumption (599,624.07 kWh) versus 50.35 % off‑peak (608,075.89 kWh). Twelve distinct meters are represented, and the highest‑consumption meter recorded 252,241.26 kWh.

limitations: The analysis relies on a single year of smart‑meter data; seasonal anomalies or multi‑year trends cannot be assessed.
Missing temperature values (62 readings) may bias the temperature‑consumption correlation.
Only three building‑type categories are present; other categories (e.g., public sector) are not represented.
Tariff classification is limited to peak vs. off‑peak; finer tariff structures are not captured.
conclusion: Industrial consumption drives the bulk of electricity use, with a modest seasonal increase in the second half of 2024. Peak and off‑peak loads are nearly balanced, suggesting opportunities for load‑shifting incentives. Hot‑day commercial demand is low, but the negative temperature‑consumption correlation indicates higher usage in cooler periods. Addressing data gaps and expanding the temporal scope will improve future demand‑side strategies.
